topic_summaries.UK Energy Bills and Fuel Poverty:
• The i and Channel 4 News focus on rising bills and cost-of-living impact, with Channel 4 highlighting fuel poverty in Shetland as a human story; Metro takes a practical consumer angle with energy-saving tips
• GB News frames energy costs as driven by policy failures ("wasted wind") and health consequences of fuel poverty; The Guardian emphasises subsidy windfalls for older renewables projects
• Channel 4 News and The i link the price spike explicitly to the Iran conflict and inflation; GB News and Metro treat rising bills as a standalone household burden
topic_summaries.Waste, Pollution and Environmental Law E:
• BBC and GB News focus on enforcement failures — illegal waste sites and criminals "running rings" around authorities; The Guardian emphasises government lawbreaking over biodiversity decline
• Daily Mail and Evening Standard both cover London air quality but from different angles — Daily Mail frames ULEZ as a failed policy, Evening Standard treats pollution as an active public health alert
• BBC gives voice to individual victims of toxic pollution (cancer, Blue Brook incident); Evening Standard focuses on a local official's personal relief at escaping flood risk
topic_summaries.COP31 Climate Negotiations:
• The Guardian dominates coverage with extensive live blogs and editorial framing around climate finance failures, fossil fuel phase-out battles, and systemic debt inequality; The Independent focuses on specific flashpoints like the wealthy-poor nation financial standoff and US Democratic re-engagement.

• Channel 4 News and The Independent humanise the crisis through frontline voices — Tuvalu islanders, indigenous Russian leaders, and vulnerable farming communities — while GB News and The Sun prioritise political embarrassment angles (Burnham's trip, Albanese's hot-mic gaffe).

• The Guardian and The Independent treat the draft deal's contested fossil fuel language as a critical breaking story; BBC coverage is notably more peripheral, focusing on a local UK youth COP event rather than the main negotiations.
topic_summaries.Fossil Fuel Industry Accountability:
• The Guardian dominates coverage, framing fossil fuel accountability across multiple angles — legal immunity threats in the US, chemical disclosure failures in Colorado, lobbying misalignment in Australia, and industry infiltration of Cop31

• The Independent takes a narrower, data-led approach, focusing specifically on Australia's continued approval of new fossil fuel projects despite its Cop31 leadership role

• Both outlets highlight institutional hypocrisy — The Guardian through figures like Panama's minister ("oil mafia") and Al Gore, The Independent through statistical evidence of government contradiction
topic_summaries.Rosebank Oilfield and North Sea Drilling:
• GB News dominates coverage, framing the Rosebank debate as a Labour internal crisis — highlighting rebellion numbers (75, then 100 MPs), ministerial hypocrisy, and accusations of being "captured by extremist green lobby"
• The Guardian presents the issue as a solvable tension between climate action and growth, taking a more constructive policy tone via Jonathan Freedland's commentary
• Daily Mail's coverage is peripheral and unfocused, with Rosebank appearing only as a secondary angle to a Greenpeace/windfarm story buried under unrelated celebrity content
topic_summaries.El Niño: Impacts and Outlook:
• The Guardian dominates coverage with a humanitarian and ecological framing — linking El Niño to maternal mortality, Indigenous flooding, Pacific island food scarcity, and marine ecosystem disruption; the Independent focuses on specific disaster events (Indonesia wildfires, Fiji drought, "Super El Niño" arrival)

• BBC and Independent emphasise El Niño's meteorological scale and future outlook, while the Daily Mail frames it as a spectacle through surfer culture

• The Guardian's most forward-looking piece frames a "super El Niño" as a "risk multiplier" ahead of COP31, giving the topic explicit climate policy urgency absent from other outlets
topic_summaries.EV Targets and UK Climate Action Plan:
• BBC and The Guardian both cover adviser warnings that weakening EV sales rules risks missing legally binding climate targets, with The Guardian adding explicit detail about the net zero 2050 deadline
• The Mirror frames EV coverage around consumer cost concerns, focusing on the potential end of cheap Chinese electric cars linked to an EU trade reset
• GB News emphasises energy dependency risks from Net Zero and local opposition to wind turbines, taking a more sceptical tone toward climate policy compared to other outlets

The Cop presidents Chris Bowen and Murat Kurum leave a press conference about the most recent draft of the cover text, which omitted any mention of fossil fuels. Photograph: Chris McGrath/Getty Images
View image in fullscreen
The Cop presidents Chris Bowen and Murat Kurum leave a press conference about the most recent draft of the cover text, which omitted any mention of fossil fuels. Photograph: Chris McGrath/Getty Images






From 4h ago


Every mention of fossil fuels has been expunged from the draft text for the main outcome of the Cop31 UN climate summit, in a blow to the vulnerable countries which had fought hard for its inclusion.
The “transition away from fossil fuels” was in the first 18-page draft, published on Monday, but missing from the second, which was released at 3pm Turkey time on Thursday. This slimmed down second draft is 9 pages long and has 80 paragraphs, in place of the 144 items previously.
There appears to be not even an oblique reference to the transition away from fossil fuels, which was agreed at Cop28 in Dubai, in a declaration known as the UAE Consensus.
But language reaffirming the global commitment to holding temperatures to 1.5C and limiting the overshoot of that target was retained.
In place of the transition away from fossil fuels, the second draft has a much weaker promise, of a “transition towards low greenhouse gas emissions and climate-resilient development”, which the Guardian noted earlier today some countries were trying to use as a weaker alternative to the fossil fuel phaseout.
This call appears twice, in some strengthened language calling for “concrete solutions to accelerate the irreversible global transition towards low greenhouse gas emissions and climate resilience, and to keep 1.5 degrees within reach, recognizing that countries will take different pathways and solutions”.
The proposed target of deriving 35% of final energy from electricity by 2035 is still in the text, but instead of being binding it is one of a suite of voluntary options countries can take “in accordance with their national circumstances and development priorities”.
This draft also calls on countries to resolve their differences over the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change so that its latest science can inform negotiations at Cop33.

articles.jina_text:
On the night of 23 October, Jimmie Goodman was trying to get some rest when his sister, who was recovering from back surgery and having trouble sleeping, woke him. Authorities in their home town of Shiprock, New Mexico, had warned that the nearby San Juan River was at risk of flooding as unprecedented rain fell across the Four Corners region of the south-west US – and so Goodman peeked outside.
“That surge shot directly at us,” said Goodman, 67, describing how the river takes a sharp 90-degree turn near his and his sister’s house in one of the Navajo housing authority’s residential neighborhoods. It just missed the house by about 50ft, he said.

As water from the river began filling their driveway, Goodman, who is Navajo/Diné, went back inside to help his sister into his green Ford pickup. The brother and sister had already loaded the truck with some essentials, but Goodman ran back inside to turn off the main power to the house and save his Taylor Swift CDs before he heard his sister call: “Let’s go!”


When he stepped back outside, Goodman’s foot sank into what he guessed was 6-8in of water. “It was like the Bellagio Casino,” he said.
After a painfully dry year that saw New Mexico record its hottest summer on record, heavy thunderstorms and rains intensified by this year’s El Niño lashed the south-west. In the Four Corners region, two weekend storms in late October and early November caused once-in-a-generation flooding in the flash-flood-prone desert. The San Juan River crested at 21ft near Shiprock, the highest it had been reported there since 1935, and reached levels not seen across much of the region since 1911. As families were ordered to evacuate, the flood waters damaged several wastewater treatment facilities in New Mexico and Utah, causing sewage to flood into the river.


View image in fullscreen
Standing flood water in Bloomfield, New Mexico, on 30 October 2026. Photograph: Ewan Adams/The Daily Lobo


“The San Juan River is a hazmat situation,” Devin Neeley, a spokesperson for San Juan county, said in late October. “Do not go in the water.”
Communities across the Four Corners region – where the 27,000 sq mile (70,000 sq km) Navajo Nation reservation stretches across parts of New Mexico, Arizona and Utah – were affected by the rains and ensuing floods. In Dennehotso, Arizona, emergency personnel rescued elders as old as 102 by raft and helicopter. Across the border near Bluff, Utah, residents were ordered to evacuate, and remained hesitant to return weeks later as E coli levels in the river and surrounding soil measured 25 times the norm. And in Rock Point, Arizona, voters decided whether to navigate hazardous muddy roads to reach the polls on election day.


View image in fullscreen
Volunteers fill sandbags and distribute them to local homeowners in Bloomfield, New Mexico, on 30 October. Photograph: Ewan Adams/The Daily Lobo

Britain risks becoming energy-dependent on China for decades unless it slows down its race to Net Zero, a new report warns. 
The UK's Net Zero policies, which include traditional power sources being replaced by wind and solar, mean that vital supplies are increasingly coming from China, think tank Policy Exchange says.








Because wind farms and large solar projects operate for more than 30 years, this supply dependence could last into the 2060s, it says.
"Decarbonisation must strengthen British strategic autonomy, rather than place its foundations in Beijing’s hands," says the report, The China Trap.




China controls around 91 per cent of UK solar imports. 
Globally, it accounts for 94 per cent of permanent-magnet manufacturing capacity, needed for wind power, and 70 per cent of battery production for electric vehicles.
In a severe crisis, losing Chinese imports could see the UK's £40 billion car export industry almost halve, while offshore wind installation could drop by 75 per cent, the report warns.

The report says that China's dominance of clean-energy supply "sits within a wider programme of strategic competition".

Full SummaryTongan Prime Minister Fatafehi Fakafānua stated at Cop31 that the world must prioritize carbon removal technology to preserve the 1.5C global warming target. The leader emphasized that nations must simultaneously curb fossil fuel use and capture carbon to address threats like sea level rise and food insecurity.
The world must seriously begin to consider carbon removal solutions in order to keep the vital global warming target of 1.5C alive, the prime minister of Tonga has told The Independent at Cop31.
Faced with massive challenges including sea level rises, saltwater intrusion that is affecting food security, coral bleaching, and worsening tropical storms, keeping the global temperature rise limited to 1.5C is considered crucial for small island states like Tonga. 
Indeed, the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) - the world’s foremost climate science body - has warned that, for some low-lying coral atoll nations in the Pacific and Indian Oceans, the difference between 1.5C and 2C of warming could determine whether they remain habitable.





The planet has, however, already breached the 1.5C target at points, according to the latest science, and is currently on track for 2.7C of warming by 2100 under current policies. That is why, according to Fatafehi Fakafānua – the youngest leader in the Pacific at 41 – the world must begin to more seriously look at solutions to bring carbon dioxide levels in the atmosphere back down. 
“We need to both curb fossil fuels and now – at the other end – capture carbon,” he said. “It needs to be all hands on deck. We need to look at the whole picture holistically to keep 1.5C alive.”

articles.jina_text:
Climate science is “foundational” to the Paris agreement and worldwide progress on tackling global heating, and attempts to delay new scientific reports threaten global cooperation on tackling the crisis, one of the world’s leading climate scientists has warned.
Johan Rockström, the director of the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research, said the world’s leading body of climate scientists, the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, must be allowed to work as quickly as possible on its next comprehensive assessment of global knowledge of the climate systems.

Some countries are holding up work on the three-part report in a row over the body’s role and representation of developing countries. One group has argued that racist assumptions underpin some of the body’s recommendations.
Rockström said the reports were fair. “The IPCC is objective, evidence-based science, and it’s the only thing that we can reliably stand on as a basis for our policymaking,” he said. “The IPCC is the summary of everything done voluntarily by scientists from the entire world, global south and global north, that collectively carries out a synthesis [of established research].”


View image in fullscreen
Rockström speaking at Cop31 this week. Photograph: Beyza Comert/Anadolu/Getty Images
The IPCC’s work is used to inform the annual climate “conference of the parties” (Cop) to the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change. Its next assessment, called AR7, the seventh in a series dating back to 1988, under way, and it is hoped it will be completed in 2028. In the autumn of that year, nations will gather for Cop33, where the second “global stocktake” under the Paris agreement will be thrashed out.


This is the mechanism by which progress towards the core Paris goal, of limiting temperature rises to 1.5C above pre-industrial levels, will be judged. The stocktake is almost certain to find that current pledges to cut greenhouse gas emissions are inadequate and must be improved.
The UN has already found the world to be on track for a 2.8C temperature rise, a level previous IPCC reports have found would result in severe and, in some cases, irreversible consequences, such as the melting of ice caps and glaciers, sea level rises, coral bleaching and extreme weather.
But some countries – chiefly Russia, India and the Arab group of countries including Saudi Arabia – want to delay publication of AR7 until 2029, after the global stocktake is completed. They argue, with the backing of some climate campaigners, that developing countries are disadvantaged in trying to submit science to the IPCC. As a result, some claim, the work is permeated by racist assumptions that guarantee the privilege of developed countries.
Lidy Nacpil, the coordinator of the Asian Peoples’ Movement on Debt and Development, told the Guardian the IPCC’s scenarios for cutting greenhouse gas emissions – known as “mitigation” in UN jargon – were “biased against the interests of the global south”.

articles.summary: Leading climate scientist Johan Rockström has warned that attempts by some countries to delay the IPCC's next comprehensive climate assessment report (AR7) threaten global cooperation on tackling the climate crisis. The IPCC report is considered foundational to the Paris agreement and is due to be completed in 2028, ahead of Cop33 where the second global stocktake will assess progress toward limiting temperature rises to 1.5C. Some countries are holding up the work over disputes about the body's role and representation of developing countries, with one group arguing that racist assumptions underpin some of its recommendations.

articles.jina_text:
The government doesn’t know what they are going to be used for, but that’s beside the point. Their real purpose is to sustain the share price of big tech




It should have the status of an economic law: the sectors a government does most to promote in the name of growth are the sectors most likely to tank the economy. In the UK and the US, deregulation was meant to turn the financial sector into a never-ending growth machine. We have not yet fully recovered from the crash it helped cause in 2008. Fossil fuels are the most heavily subsidised sector on Earth. All that public money makes us highly vulnerable to oil price shocks, the whims of autocrats and societal collapse caused by climate breakdown. As for the great growth priority of our time – AI and datacentres – well, don’t take it from me. As Anthropic’s IPO prospectus warns, advanced AI systems could pose “catastrophic or existential risks to humanity”.
One thing we learned from the US midterm elections is that the drive to build datacentres is less a function of real commercial demand than of the need to sustain the share price of the big tech companies. After citizens across the US voted for moratoria on new datacentres, tech stocks, which have become dangerously dominant, plummeted, triggering fears of wider contagion. Whether new datacentres are required or not, we must keep building them, because confidence depends on them, and without that confidence the bubble will pop. The more you build, and the more this value dependency grows, the bigger the bubble becomes.



This could be why, combined with its catastrophic reliance on commercial lobbyists to tell it what to think, the UK government has enabled datacentres to be classified as “nationally significant infrastructure”, allowing them to swerve local planning control and go straight to ministers for approval. This, the government reasons, is because they are critical to future growth. But growth of what? Some good things, to be sure. But also – and perhaps predominantly – of gambling and pornography, which includes paedophiles nudifying children’s images. Reports of this crime have risen by 8,400% in the past two years, and it has doubtless contributed to that infallible measure of public wellbeing, GDP. Other beneficiaries might include shitposters, fascists using algorithms to boost their content and Russian cyber-attackers.
The government has admitted that while it grants critical special dispensation to these datacentres, it doesn’t know what they are going to be used for. But their ostensible purpose is beside the point. Their real purpose is to sustain the growth in tech shares: growth that could trigger economic collapse.
This is why you must do your duty before God and country, by allowing a vast, roaring, windowless box to loom over your home. This is why you must put your objections aside, and let it destroy your landscape and local character, block out the sun by day and flood the night sky with light, suck the water out

Full SummaryFiji declared a national state of disaster following an El Nino-driven drought that caused widespread water shortages, with the government setting aside 20 million Fiji dollars for emergency response. Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka stated the declaration allows for mobilized resources to assist families and farmers as conditions worsen.
Fiji has declared a national state of disaster after an El Nino-driven drought caused widespread water shortages, with the Pacific nation's weather bureau forecasting below-normal rainfall until at least April. 
In a national address on Wednesday, prime minister Sitiveni Rabuka said ⁠the declaration would allow his government to scale up its response by mobilising resources and coordinating assistance as conditions continue to worsen.
"Families across Fiji are concerned about the availability of water and the effects of prolonged dry conditions on their daily lives," Mr Rabuka said. 





"Farmers ​are ⁠worried about their crops and livestock, while communities, particularly in remote and maritime areas, face growing pressure on their water ⁠supplies. These concerns are real."
Mr Rabuka said his government has set aside 20 million Fiji dollars ($8.5m) for the national response, redeployed from existing funds, to ensure emergency water supplies for families and farmers. The state of disaster has been declared for ‌one month, with the government able to extend ‌or revoke it based on the advice of the National Disaster Risk Management Council.

articles.title: Inflation and energy prices rise – how high could it get?
articles.raw_rss: Inflation has risen to its highest level for a year with spiralling petrol and diesel prices largely to blame.
articles.raw_content:
Inflation has risen to its highest level for a year with spiralling petrol and diesel prices largely to blame.
It’s now running at 3.6 per cent, up from 3.5 per cent in September, with a warning from the Bank of England it could peak at around 5 per cent next year.
Diesel prices have risen by 7 pence per litre to an average of just under £2 – the highest figure since records from the Office for National Statistics began 30 years ago.
And another factor driving further inflation, a prediction today of a sharp hike in energy costs early next year from the consultancy firm, Cornwall Insight.  They warn the annual price cap on gas and electricity may rise by 26% from January.
It’s a jump which would put an extra £443 on the average bill – a most unwelcome early Christmas present.

World ‘held hostage by oil mafia’, says Panama minister at Cop 31


Key issues unresolved as summit enters final days, with 30 countries signed up to forge fossil fuel treaty separate to UN process




The world is “being held hostage by the petroleum mafia” and seems unable to break free, Panama’s environment minister has warned, as key issues remain unresolved in the final days of the UN Cop31 climate summit.
“We are in love with our kidnappers,” said Juan Carlos Navarro, at a press conference to announce 30 countries were now signed up to forge a new fossil fuel treaty, separate to the UN process. “We love the petroleum guys. We can’t live without them, and they are so smart they have convinced us that they are doing this for our own good.”

Expressing the frustration shared by scores of developing countries and thousands of civil society activists at these talks, he added: “They torture us for our own good, they destroy our planet for our own good. They destroy nature to help us, and they demand our unrequited, endless, unlimited, boundless love. And we are so stupid that we fall for it.”


Countries have only two official days of negotiation left at Cop31 to resolve key issues, such as whether the conference should recognise the need to “transition away from fossil fuels” and how to address the “overshoot” of global temperatures beyond the 1.5C of heating targeted in the Paris agreement.
The Australian presidency of the talks and the Turkish hosts convened a “divan” meeting of ministers on Wednesday evening. Named for the Ottoman empire’s term for a council or assembly, the aim of the meeting was to make progress on a revised draft of a possible outcome and find compromises on sticking points. Significant dividing lines remain on issues such as climate finance, how to ensure a “just transition” to clean economy jobs for workers in fossil fuels and helping poor countries adapt to the impacts of extreme weather.
The first draft of a “cover decision”, issued on Monday, contained 144 separate items, including several – such as the “transition away from fossil fuels” – that some of the nearly 200 countries at the fortnight-long talks find contentious. There are concerns that the Australian approach of including “everything” in the draft text may result in longer negotiations. A new draft is expected on Thursday morning.


A breakthrough from the “divan” meeting was not expected, but negotiators told the Guardian that countries were working together on compromises. Campaigners feared that the outcome would be feeble, however.

articles.title: All the cost of living help you can get this winter as energy bills to rise by £443
articles.raw_rss: From £100-household payments to energy discounts and emergency grants, here is the support available to help with rising costs
articles.raw_content:
Millions of households are set to face a blow later this winter as energy costs could soar by £443 a year from January 2027.



A new forecast, from energy consultancy Cornwall Insight, suggests energy bills could go up 26 per cent as of 1 January,  from £1,723 to £2,166, as the Iran war pushes up wholesale prices.



Ofgem will confirm the cap for January to March on 25 November.



Simon Francis, co-ordinator of the End Fuel Poverty Coalition, said: “It now looks like households will pay more for every unit of gas this winter than at any point in history.”



But what help is available, and how much could you save? 



£100-household energy payment



Up to 20 million households in England could receive a £100 payment from January 2027 to help with energy costs.



It is available to households whose main home falls within council tax bands A to D, including most households exempt from council tax.



Those who pay council tax by direct debit should automatically receive the money into their bank account. Others can apply through their local council.



The Government has also allocated £100m to councils to support households that do not qualify for the standard payment, including some in higher council tax bands.



Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland are also set to receive additional funding, with their governments deciding how to distribute support.



£150 Warm Home Discount



A £150 energy bill discount is available for eligible low-income households through the War

The COP climate talks are into their second week in Antalya, Turkey. For the last five years, this programme has been following the story of Tuvalu, the Pacific island nation midway between Australia and Hawaii that’s likely to be one of the first to disappear entirely under the rising ocean.
While its leaders push for an end to the burning of fossil fuels, their people are starting to relocate to Australia.
We’ve been to meet Tuvaluans who’ve moved to Brisbane to find out how they’re adapting to life away from their islands. And we caught up with the youth activist Grace Malie who’s attending the COP summit.

The U.S. has officially lost its measles-elimination status as the virus spreads uninterrupted among unvaccinated populations at the fastest rate in over three decades. 
The current surge represents the worst U.S. measles outbreak since 1991, with more than 7,000 cases and 11 deaths over the last two years, driven heavily by a major outbreak in Pennsylvania. 
Public health experts attribute the resurgence to declining immunization rates falling below the required 95% community coverage threshold, alongside growing vaccine hesitancy and misinformation. 
Vaccination rates have been falling against a number of diseases, in the U.S. and globally and experts caution that other vaccine-preventable diseases could follow measles in re-emergence.
“It can be the canary in the coal mine to other things,” said Dr. Susan Kansagra, chief medical officer of the Association of State and Territorial Health Officials.

COP31 climate summit is taking place in Turkiye’s Antalya Photograph: Ayse Eda Unlu Ozen/Anadolu/Getty Images
The Cop31 climate summit in Antalya is in its final days, and negotiators are fighting over a first draft of the deal.
It calls for “accelerated action to phase out fossil fuels, including through the immediate transition away from fossil fuels in energy systems”, and for tripling adaptation finance for poorer countries. But with the world heading past the 1.5C limit and countries deeply divided over finance, adaptation and the “just transition”, can Cop31 deliver anything that matters?
The Guardian’s environment editor, Fiona Harvey, reported that the 18-page draft contains 144 separate items, many of which are unlikely to survive: “There are still at least four and a half days of heavy negotiating to go, so this text will go through many more iterations.” Campaigners are sceptical. Tzeporah Berman of the Fossil Fuel Non-Proliferation Treaty Initiative said: “This mention in the draft text will last about 2 minutes and they know it.”
Ministers have now arrived in Antalya to start cutting the text down. Chris Bowen, the Australian minister presiding over the talks, admitted: “The first draft will look very different to the final draft.”
At the opening leaders’ summit, Hilda Heine, president of the Marshall Islands, warned: “Our response to the threat of overshoot must be overwhelming, or the world we know is over.” The UN secretary general, António Guterres, put it more bluntly: “It’s make or bake time.” Yet only 91 national leaders attended, and Donald Trump and Xi Jinping were among those absent.
The Guardian’s editorial argued that those pushing for a faster shift away from fossil fuels “are on the side of the future, while their opponents are stuck in the past”.
What do you want to know about what’s happening in Antalya? Can a summit co-hosted by an oil-producing Turkey and a coal-exporting Australia get a fossil-fuel phaseout over the line? That’s all for today. Here are the highlights from the ninth day of the 31st UN climate summit:
 
 
Yesterday’s draft deal exposed thorny divisions as negotiations head into the final days  
 
Popular AI chatbots quickly turn to climate denial, a UN-backed study found  
 
Russia, Saudi Arabia and Australia are the biggest historical exporters of fossil fuel emissions, analysis found  
 
The EU’s climate commissioner described the latest draft as a “shopping list” that was fundamentally at odds with the logic of delivering previous agreements  
 
The UK signed on to a statement urging polluters to pay, as countries explore the use of targeted levies to claw back money for climate action from those responsible

Full SummaryDemocratic leaders at the Cop31 climate conference in Antalya, Turkey, are working to build a platform for a US climate return following the midterm election results that impacted Donald Trump. The 'America Is All In' delegation includes approximately 120 officials seeking to maintain climate discussions despite the US withdrawal from the Paris Agreement.
For Emily Randall, the recently re-elected representative for Washington state's 6th Congressional district, the justification for attending the Cop31 climate conference in Antalya, Turkey, could not be clearer. 
“Working-class communities in my district are facing prohibitively expensive insurance as the sea level rises and flooding increases,” she says. “I also have a lot of tribal nations that are having to move their villages uplands because of the sea level rises… I also have the Olympic National Forest, which is one of the old growth lungs of our planet, which we want to do everything we can to protect.”
A pressing awareness of climate challenges has also brought Janet Cowell – a fellow Democrat and mayor of Raleigh, North Carolina – to the climate conference. “We are in the middle of a hurricane zone, and we are facing more and more droughts, and it is incredibly hot,” she says. “These things are becoming daily conversations where people are concerned.” 





Representative Randall and Mayor Cowell have come to Antalya as members of the “America Is All In” delegation: a group of some 120 US governors, mayors, local officials and members of Congress who are looking to fill the US-shaped hole in climate discussions after President Donald Trump decided to withdraw his country from the UN climate convention and exited the landmark Paris Agreement.

Where do people want to see Britain’s climate action plan working? On their own doorstep

Miatta Fahnbulleh



I am at Cop 31 – concerned about the crisis around the world, but mindful that voters want jobs, warmer homes and cheaper prices


Miatta Fahnbulleh is the UK secretary of state for energy security and net zero




In this cold weather, it is easy to forget that Britain has just been through its hottest summer on record, part of our new reality as the climate crisis reaches our doorstep. For millions around the world, the consequences have already been more devastating for the communities that did the least to cause this crisis.
That is the backdrop to Cop31 in Antalya, Turkey, where I arrive on Tuesday as the UK’s chief negotiator. As I have prepared for these negotiations, I’ve been reflecting on the gap between the science and the political debate in Britain. Early predictions by the Met Office indicate that 2027 will surpass 2024 as the hottest year on record globally as El Niño rips through the Pacific. This is a sobering reality. And yet, the Conservatives and Reform UK want to bury their heads in the sand and break the consensus on delivering net zero. But we know sustained climate action can work.



Yes, the world will overshoot 1.5C of global heating in the coming years. But without the Paris agreement, the world would have been on track for a 4C increase. International commitments, finance and adaptation are working, and multilateralism has never been more vital to our future. Every fraction of a degree we prevent means lives protected and communities given a better chance at surviving. Setbacks bring frustration, but resistance is the sign of progress.
Britain has a responsibility to lead, and we are determined to do so. I am proud of the progress we have made to cut emissions by 54% since 1990 and the action we are taking to achieve net zero by 2050. And I am equally proud of our record on climate action abroad. We exceeded our five-year international climate finance commitment, spending £12.8bn between 2021-22 and 2025-26 against a pledge of £11.6bn. Britain exceeded its £3bn nature target and tripled annual adaptation funding from £500m to more than £1.5bn.
And the real measure of that investment is what it has achieved. Since 2011, UK climate finance has helped an estimated 159 million people across the world better adapt to the climate crisis, reduced or avoided 201m tonnes of greenhouse gas emissions and mobilised about £26bn in public and private finance.

Farmers are utilising science and nature to help orchards adapt and thrive in the face of shifting temperatures, rainfall and pests




On Myrtle Farm in Somerset, there are thousands of apple trees laid out in rows of 100. Over the past year, each has endured the same wet winter and long summer drought. Now, the different ways each tree responded to these challenges are being analysed in trials that could shape the future of apple growing – and the taste of cider – for decades to come.
Myrtle Farm is the home of Thatchers Cider, which this year had its earliest ever harvest in the company’s 122-year history. Yet the farm’s experimental orchard of 3,800 trees, where each 100-tree row produces a different apple variety, offers hope that – even as the climate emergency deepens – future harvests will become more consistent and predictable.

The trials aim to identify robust apple varieties that are resistant to diseases and pests, crop reliably and can withstand the most extreme weather that might affect Somerset.


View image in fullscreen

 
 
Two apples ripe for harvest, which this year ran from the middle of August to November at Myrtle Farm  
“Somerset is the best county in the world for making cider. But the climate is changing. It has been changing for a long time. We need to be in a position where we’ve got the experience, the knowledge and the trees in place to deal with those changes,” says Martin Thatcher, the company’s managing director.
One of the biggest challenges he faces is the length of time it takes to introduce a new apple variety and change growing methods in orchards. “It doesn’t happen overnight. Each apple tree takes seven years to get to a fruit crop and could last 40 years. So it takes a very long time [for experiments] to come to fruition,” he says.
The trials came about because, nearly 30 years ago, his father, John Thatcher, rescued 458 varieties of cider apples grown at the Long Ashton research station, a government-funded horticultural and agricultural research centre founded in 1903. “My father took cuttings of every single variety before the centre was closed down, so we have an orchard with 458 varieties in it.”


View image in fullscreen

 
 
Nestled by the Mendips, the Shiplate orchard, near Bleadon, has more than 65,000 trees across 57 hectares (140 acres)  
The collection includes traditional cider apples and newer varieties that cater for modern tastes. “We’re looking at that orchard now and first of all seeing which apples make fabulous cider. And then we’re looking at how the trees are doing under modern orchard conditions – and if they’re good healthy trees and they’re cropping, we will plant them out in rows of 100-tree trials, to future-proof our orchard growing.”

Fifa accused of climate ‘record of failure’ due to Aramco deal and tournament expansion




Groups question ‘sincerity’ to meet emissions pledges

Oil giant is a major sponsor of football governing body




The United Nations has been asked to review Fifa’s status as a signatory to a key environmental initiative, with complainants arguing football’s governing body has a “record of failure” on climate action.
Fifa is a signatory to the UN’s Sports for Climate Action Framework, a coalition which seeks to persuade sporting organisations to “work together to achieve a climate-resilient future”. Under the framework, signatories agree to cut their greenhouse gas emissions by 50% by 2030 and to “partner with key stakeholders to deliver joint climate action”. They can have their status as a signatory removed, however, if “sincerity in participation or ability to participate is a cause for concern”.








Cop31 summit spells out stark warnings for athletes and sport organisations

Read more
According to five organisations that have submitted a joint complaint to the UN, Fifa’s actions are inconsistent with its words. In a letter to executives at the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change, they argue “being a signatory of the Framework means making a commitment to both organisational climate progress and climate leadership. On the basis of the facts laid out below, we assert that Fifa has a record of failure on each of these key commitments.”
The letter claims Fifa has undermined its commitments by expanding the size of its tournaments, with the men’s World Cup increasing from 64 matches in 2022 to 104 matches in 16 cities across three countries this past summer, making it what the complainants say is “the most polluting World Cup ever”. In 2030, by which time Fifa’s emissions should have been halved, the World Cup is due to be held in six countries across three different continents, with potentially 64 teams and even more matches.


The complainants acknowledge Fifa launched a climate strategy in 2021, committing it to halving emissions by 2030 and reaching net zero by 2040. “However,” the letter says, “that strategy is not clear on how exactly these targets will be achieved. The evidence indicates that Fifa has expanded, rather than reduced, its emissions in the years since, principally by choosing to expand the footprint of its major tournaments.”

articles.jina_text:
Russia, Saudi Arabia and Australia are the three biggest exporters of carbon dioxide in history, according to analysis of fossil fuels since 1850.
Russia tops the list of global exporters of fossil fuels, with its vast coal, oil and gas deposits. Accounting for the CO2 produced by burning these exports, Russia has been responsible for more than 70 gigatonnes, up to the end of 2025.

Saudi Arabia, one of the world’s biggest producers of oil and gas, comes next with about 60 gigatonnes of CO2 exported. The country has long been an obstructive force at the annual UN climate summits.
Australia is in third place, a long way behind the top two exporters, with responsibility for more than 25 gigatonnes of exported CO2, not far ahead of Venezuela. The revelation comes as Australia acts as president of this year’s UN climate summit, Cop31, which is now into its second week in Turkey. The country has yet to set an end point for the use or export of fossil fuels, which make up about two-fifths of its export economy.

Louise Hutchins, the convener of the Make Polluters Pay International Coalition, said: “This analysis tells you a lot about what’s going wrong with climate negotiations. Here at Cop31, governments claim there’s not enough money to tackle the climate crisis, while Australia, Russia and Saudi Arabia, that have amassed fortunes from fossil fuels, continue to wield pivotal political power in this consensus-based process.


“Just look at Australia. Its contribution to global heating more than doubles when fossil fuel exports are counted. Yet it is co-presiding over the very negotiations where climate finance talks are once again in stalemate.
“Responsibility is on the wealthy, the powerful and the profiteers. Those who made fortunes from fossil fuels must pay for the damage.”
The analysis of historical exports of fossil fuels, conducted by Carbon Brief and seen by the Guardian, apportions responsibility for CO2 emissions based on the country extracting the fossil fuels, in contrast to most analyses, which look to the countries where the CO2 is released.
Calculating where the fossil fuels came from casts the global economy, and historical responsibilities for emissions, in a new light. Exporting countries can be relatively low on the list of global greenhouse gas emitters, because those calculations are based on fossil fuel use.
The analysis also shows that the US and China – the world’s two biggest current emitters of greenhouse gases – still bear greater responsibility for historical emissions than Russia, Saudi or Australia, because as well as importing vast quantities of fossil fuels, they have also burned their own supplies.



The Cop28 UN conference outcome in Dubai in 2023 called on all countries to contribute to a global fossil fuel transition, but set no timetable or workplan for doing so. This is just the beginning …
For two years, Americans have witnessed a largely unchecked assault on the foundations of US democracy. While enriching themselves through flagrant corruption, the president and his allies have launched aggressive attacks on press freedom, voting rights, due process and many other fundamental civil rights. And they have shown a troubling disregard for the truth.
On election day, America’s embattled democracy came roaring back to life: from Texas to Ohio to South Carolina, a majority of Americans rejected this path at the ballot box. The voting public claimed its right to hold power to account, and millions are now looking at politics with a new and unfamiliar feeling of hope. 
The past two years demonstrated just how fragile our fundamental freedoms are, when precious few powerful institutions are willing to stand up for them. Major law firms and universities capitulated to a bullying president’s threats and intimidation. Some corporate news outlets bowed to his pressure, too.
In this atmosphere of fear, the independent press stood out as one of the only forces for accountability, dedicated to uncovering the truth – and to making sure the public understood what was at stake in the election.
A free press has an essential role to play in a robust democracy, shedding light on hidden schemes and revealing the whole picture of our flawed world. Yet these are challenging times for press freedom: Trump’s crackdown on the press shows no signs of letting up; consolidated ownership means fewer options and less diversity of perspective; and the AI industry has threatened the entire business model of journalism, resulting in extreme staff layoffs that have gutted newsrooms.
We will need a free press in 2027 as much as we relied on one in 2025 and 2026. The Guardian is fortunate to have no billionaire owner, no corporate bosses who put profit over mission. We’re accountable to the facts and to our readers. And the Guardian is fortunate to have readers who are willing to support – and commit month after month – to help sustain our independence.

Experts said the shift in sea turtle nests was likely driven by this year’s El Niño conditions. Photograph: Robin Riggs/Aquarium of the Pacific


Band of baby sea turtles swims into ocean after historic California nesting


Hatchlings emerge after discovery in September of first sea turtle nests ever to have been recorded on US west coast




Two months after the discovery of the first sea turtle nests ever to have been recorded on the US west coast, the eggs have hatched – and California’s first group of 75 native-born olive ridley sea turtles have been released into the Pacific.
The eggs incubated at the Aquarium of the Pacific in Long Beach after the historic discovery of two separate nests in September at southern California beaches, a shift likely driven by this year’s El Niño conditions.

On Saturday, the Aquarium of the Pacific announced the turtles’ first emergence in a social media post: “The hatchlings are here! We are excited to share that some of the olive ridley sea turtle eggs from Seal Beach successfully hatched after a 58-day incubation period. Working with our partners, we carefully released them from the beach in the dark early hours of this morning.”
A day later, the Aquarium added: “Even more egg-citing news! A second group of olive ridley sea turtle hatchlings, this time from the Huntington Beach nest, was released into the ocean early Sunday morning.”


View image in fullscreen
Olive ridley sea turtle hatchlings are released in Huntington Beach, California. Photograph: Robin Riggs/Aquarium of the Pacific
In total, 54 turtles were released from the Seal Beach nest and 21 from the Huntington Beach nest.


On 16 September, an olive ridley sea turtle was observed digging a nest and laying eggs on Seal Beach in the first-recorded instance of any sea turtle nesting on the west coast. Three days later, a second turtle was spotted nesting on Huntington Beach.
Typically a tropical species, the olive ridley sea turtle normally resides in the Pacific, Indian and Atlantic oceans, but has been known to nest on the southern tip of Baja California.
“It is not known why these turtles chose southern California beaches as nesting sites, but it indicates an important historical change that could have long-term implications for the species and for local sea turtle management and protection,” the Aquarium of the Pacific said in a social media post.
“The behavior of these turtles was probably influenced, at least in part, by the incoming El Niño, along with the recent tropical storm, range expansion, or perhaps navigational mistakes. The species is also known for its behavioral flexibility.”

Full SummaryA first draft of the Cop31 deal text has drawn criticism from climate campaigners for lacking clarity and containing contradictory proposals, according to observers. The 18-page document includes competing formulations on fossil fuels and a target for electricity to account for 35 per cent of global energy by 2035. Negotiations face a Friday deadline to reach an agreement.
A first draft of text for a deal at Cop31 has been circulated to delegates, drawing swift criticism from climate campaigners and reflecting the wider disarray that has characterised the largest ever UN climate summit.
As the event entered its second week on Monday, negotiations shifted from technical discussions to high-level political talks, with the cover decision intended to set out the key outcomes countries hope to secure.
But the 18-page, 144-paragraph draft appears to be a sprawling compilation of most of the competing priorities put forward by countries participating in the negotiations, quickly categorised by observers as being too long, lacking clarity, and with “a lot of weeds that need to be pulled out,” according to Mohamed Adow of think tank Power Shift Africa. 





It is “best described as a mish-mash of contradictory proposals that stand little chance of making it into the final outcome text,” says Asad Rehman, chief executive of Friends of the Earth. 
“The draft text makes the right diagnosis, but the medicine it offers could have deadly side effects,” adds Romain Ioualalen of advocate group Oil Change International. “You cannot diagnose fossil fuels as the sickness and let fossil fuels be part of the care.”

articles.jina_text:
A draft text of a possible final outcome from the Cop31 UN climate summit is an attempt to “draw out parties” on their areas of agreement and disagreement, Australia’s president of the talks has said.
Many countries were surprised to see a first draft of a potential “cover decision” from the fortnight-long talks early on Monday afternoon, with more than four days of negotiation still to go. The text includes several proposals regarded as highly contentious by some countries, including a call to “immediately transition away from fossil fuels”.

Chris Bowen, Australia’s climate and energy minister, said: “It’s a genuine attempt to draw out parties on what they can support and what they can’t. There’ll be things in there that don’t have agreement, but if we only concentrated on the things that do have broad agreement, it would be a very thin document.”


The 18-page draft, which is likely to undergo several more iterations before the scheduled end of the talks on Friday evening, includes among its 144 separate items a call to “immediately transition away from fossil fuels”, and to limit the “overshoot” of the 1.5C temperature limit targeted in the Paris climate agreement.
The document in its current form lays out the competing positions of governments from tiny island states to oil behemoths and emerging economies. It needs ultimate approval by the nearly 200 nations at the UN climate summit.






Australia’s climate change minister Chris Bowen announces first draft of Cop31 deal – video


“We’ve got to start with a broad document, concentrate on getting agreement with some difficult issues, then refine it down over the coming days,” Bowen told the Guardian in an interview.
Alden Mayer, a senior associate at the E3G thinktank, said putting out the draft text at this stage was a gamble. “But it would also be a gamble to wait until later in the week. They have decided to take the ‘full monty’ approach, knowing that many of the 144 paragraphs will not survive the week,” he said. “The question is where does the presidency think the sweet spot is on the various contested issues.”
The wording on fossil fuels echoes a pledge made by all countries at Cop28 in Dubai to “transition away from fossil fuels”, which had no timetable or work programme attached, but is likely to be attacked by oil-producing countries that have hardened their positions since then.
There are also provisions to address the “overshoot” of the 1.5C temperature limit targeted in the Paris agreement and a target to derive 35% of global final energy from electricity by 2035, a key priority for the host nation, Turkey.
Mohamed Adow, the director of the Power Shift Africa thinktank, called the text “an overgrown garden. There are lots of encouraging green shoots but there are also a lot of weeds that need to be pulled out.”

articles.jina_text:
The report was launched at the UN climate summit in Antalya, Turkey on Monday.  Photograph: Mehmet Ali Ozcan/Anadolu/Getty Images
View image in fullscreen
The report was launched at the UN climate summit in Antalya, Turkey on Monday.  Photograph: Mehmet Ali Ozcan/Anadolu/Getty Images


AI models ‘weak and fallible’ on climate science, UN-backed study reports


While mostly accurate describing simple facts, models pivoted to denial and wrong answers when challenged 
 
 
Cop31 live – latest updates  




Artificial intelligence models can quickly turn into climate crisis deniers at the mildest challenge from users, according to a new UN-backed study.
While AI models can accurately confirm simple facts about climate change, eight times out of 10 when they pivoted to a wrong answer, they did so “at the very first sign that the user mildly disagreed” to confirm incorrect statements such as “CO2 is not the main driver of climate change”.

The report uncovered a strong tendency for AI models to be sycophantic, meaning the model is more interested in pleasing the user than standing by facts – an issue identified when people turn to AI chatbots for personal advice.
The report from Unesco and University College London was launched at the UN climate summit in Turkey on Monday, revealing the results of tests on 15 of the world’s most popular AI models.
Leona Verdadero, Unesco’s lead author of the report, said: “AI is not neutral. When it comes to how it responds to the user, it will be pushed to align with the users’ preference instead of sticking up for the facts. The fact they could so easily abandon truth and be more agreeable to a user’s [misinformation] shows it is weak and fallible.”
When AI was asked how a single climate policy would work, such as a carbon tax, the models were mostly accurate. But when asked how two climate policies could work together, accuracy collapsed to no better than random guessing, the researchers said.
Dr María Pérez-Ortiz, of UCL’s department of computer science and a senior author of the report, said: “AI systems are remarkably good at explaining scientific knowledge, but this can give us a false sense of their capabilities. Our findings show why we must be careful when moving from asking AI what we know about climate change to asking what we should do about it.”


View image in fullscreen
The report was published the same day Turkey, the Cop31 hosts, launched the AI Antalya pledge to make AI ‘part of the climate solution’. Photograph: Mehmet Ali Ozcan/Anadolu/Getty Images
AI models also had a language problem. Accuracy was scored at 88% for people using English, and comparatively high in Spanish, French and Portuguese.
Responses were less accurate for people speaking Hindi, Bengali and Urdu, and the worst for Swahili speakers, at 78%. This was particularly important, the report authors said, because those languages were spoken in places among the hardest hit by the climate crisis.

Surge of US datacenters adds equivalent of Denmark’s annual emissions, study finds


‘Hyperscaler’ datacenters across country draw upon dirtier power sources to meet vast energy needs, research shows




The frantic buildout of “hyperscaler” datacenters in the US has collectively caused planet-heating emissions of about the same scale as Denmark emits in a year, new research has found.
In that period 403 “hyperscalers” – the largest datacenters used primarily to handle the growth of artificial intelligence – emitted about 25.7m metric tons of carbon dioxide, according to the study.

This is equivalent to the entire annual carbon pollution of Denmark, a country of 6 million people, and is about two to three times more than a previous estimate of hyperscale emissions in 2018. The latest research, published in Nature Sustainability, found that these datacenters were responsible for about 1.8% of total US electricity consumption.
Researchers said this vast datacenter energy demand, centered on states such as Virginia, Oregon, Ohio and Iowa, is almost certainly a conservative estimate. The study used federal government data to determine emissions from the facilities over a year until April 2025. Since then, the rapid expansion of datacenters has only accelerated further.







Several Democrats renew calls for datacenter pauses after blue wave

Read more
“There has been an explosion in these datacenters and the CO2 emissions are pretty substantial,” said Francesca Dominici, a professor of biostatistics at Harvard University and co-author of the study, which was led by Gianluca Guidi. “Since 2025 there have been many, many more datacenters so we need to think of this level of emissions as a lower bound. This is something that needs study and for policymakers to think about how to do this in a responsible way.”
Datacenters use an enormous amount of energy – the new study estimates the hyperscale group consumed 68 to 99 terawatt-hours of electricity over the year – and largely draws upon dirtier sources of power to meet this demand.


More than half of the generation used by hyperscalers came from the fossil fuels that are dangerously overheating our planet, the research found. The growth of AI is being underpinned by a rise in new gas-fired power, sometimes built at the site of the facilities themselves, which is being favored over installed renewables such as solar and wind.

It would be a “serious mistake” to pass a contentious bipartisan bill to speed up energy projects and datacenters that has divided Democrats and environmentalists, Al Gore said.
The legislation, known as the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (Baaja), will make it easier to build large infrastructure projects in the US, from oil and gas pipelines and datacenters to crucial clean energy components such as solar and wind power and transmission lines, scaling back environmental protections and legal challenges in order to do so.

articles.jina_text:
Imran Lodhi is a university lecturer with a doctorate in climate change and sustainable development. The 41-year-old was living in Dera Ghazi Khan, a city in south-western Punjab, when floods devastated provinces across Pakistan. Climate change made the monsoon rainfall that caused the floods more intense.
In 2022, I was living in an area that had less risk of flooding. I had a small child and my PhD thesis was just a few weeks away. I tried to avoid flood news on social media until I saw a picture of a two-year-old girl who was buried in mud. It was probably her last breath. She died after that. That was the turning point.


View image in fullscreen
Imran Lodhi immediately rallied friends to help victims of the devastating flooding across Pakistan in 2022. Photograph: Zoral Naik
I immediately called my friends, six to seven people, in a mosque. I talked to them: “We don’t know what to do, but at least we can start from somewhere.” Initially, it was food. We hired some commercial cooks.
We planned to work only in villages close to our city. A lot of people were taking refuge in nearby high places, high enough that the water did not reach them. On the first day we went with some food to the nearest village.
When the rain is over, the sun comes out. Usually, it’s a good sign. But, in those areas, it didn’t feel good. It felt like it opened a scar. The pain that was hiding somehow had become open. It was like being naked. I could see trolleys, tractors, vehicles and homes all drowned in the flood. There was nothing from the government, nothing from any development sector. There was no camp. People were just living under open skies.
Men felt that their women being in an open place was a kind of emotional damage for them. It was not normal for most of the people here. Many women never came out. They came out for their work, the agriculture work, but not sitting that openly among the public. Their hair was full of dust and dry mud. Their clothes had a heavy layer of dry mud; no shoes on their feet. Mothers were not breastfeeding. Babies crying for milk, and the milk was not there. Mothers trying to soothe them with fake sounds.
The cows did not have feed and were not giving milk. Many of the animals were lost, their bodies wide open, decomposed. Then the water, which stayed there for a week, started to smell very bad. There was no good smell.

Great Britain’s oldest renewables projects could rake in nearly £9bn next year


Subsidy scheme, which is paid via taxes and energy bills, must be reformed, ECU analysis finds 
 
 
Business live – latest updates  




Great Britain’s oldest renewable energy projects are likely to rake in a near £9bn windfall next year because of soaring market prices, according to independent analysis.
The research has revealed that almost a third of the UK’s wind and solar farms that rely on the government’s legacy renewables subsidy scheme are in line for soaring subsidy payments as officials grapple with plans to lower the country’s energy costs.








Greenpeace boulders may delay building of £12bn windfarms in North Sea

Read more
Renewable energy projects built between 2003 and 2014 are expected to claim £4.5bn in subsidies over the next financial year, on top of £4.2bn in wholesale market revenue. The analysis showed developers will receive almost 50% more than before Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine sent gas prices soaring in 2022.
The analysis by the Energy Competitiveness Unit (ECU), a non-partisan research and policy project, said the legacy support scheme – which is paid via taxes and energy bills – must be reformed “if we are serious about getting costs of the electricity system down in the short and medium term”.
Unlike newer renewable energy projects that earn fixed-price subsidies for their generation, older projects access support via the renewables obligation (RO) scheme, which provides payments on top of what developers earn via the wholesale market, meaning that higher gas market prices lead to higher subsidy costs for renewables.
The scheme was credited with kickstarting the UK’s renewable energy industry when it was put in place almost 25 years ago, but the ECU said it “has been allowed to persist unsustainably”.
Andrew O’Brien, the ECU director, told the Guardian that the rise in wholesale prices over recent years has meant that many renewable energy developers are earning “well above what they could reasonably have expected” when first taking the decision to invest in the projects.

A solar farm near Andover in Hampshire. Photograph: Toby Melville/Reuters
The government announced last year that it would remove three-quarters of the RO scheme’s costs from home energy bills, and move these levies into general taxation from April 2026 to help temper the steep rise in energy bills.

articles.jina_text:
The Cop31 climate talks have acquired something their delegates scarcely expected: a little political breathing space. The comeback by Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in the second round of Brazil’s presidential race was important for many reasons. Victory for his opponent, Flávio Bolsonaro, would have marked a dangerous retreat from democracy. But Mr Bolsonaro’s commitment to environmental deregulation would also have spelled disaster for the Amazon, making Lula’s re-election a big win for the climate. Similarly, success by Democrats in the US midterms means that Donald Trump’s destructive grip has been loosened. If they win back the White House in 2028, the US should rejoin the UN process in time for Cop34.
While the diplomatic picture is less bleak than it might have been, the threat level remains high and rising. António Guterres used his last Cop as UN secretary general to issue a pithy warning that “it’s make or bake time”. With the latest analysis pointing to heating of 2.7C by the end of the century – far beyond the 1.5C target in the Paris agreement – governments face another crunch moment: by pivoting away from fossil fuels, they can still avert the most dangerous impacts. Yet the UK’s Andy Burnham was the only G7 leader to make the trip to Turkey; the French and German leaders chose to attend an EU summit in Dublin instead.



View image in fullscreen
António Guterres. Photograph: AFP/Getty
Warnings of mounting risks, unprecedented heat and disasters such as August’s glacier collapse on the Nepal-Tibet border can engender a sense of paralysis or unreality. The leaders of both host countries prompted anger last week: the Turkish president, Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, publicly extolled his country’s oil reserves, while Australia’s Anthony Albanese failed to mention fossil fuels in his speech. But for all its flaws, the UN climate process remains crucial. There is no other mechanism to broker a global green transition.
Mr Burnham’s appointment of a climate security adviser, Madeleine Alessandri, should focus minds in the UK. Kemi Badenoch’s rejection of net zero has undermined an important cross‑party consensus. Ministers, who must soon make a decision on Rosebank oil and gas field, must realise that economic damage caused by the carbon pollution from the oil and gas produced would dwarf any benefits. Governments of countries that are far poorer than the UK cannot be expected to turn away from coal and oil if rich countries keep investing.


A resolution to derive 35% of energy worldwide from electricity by 2035 will be agreed this week if objections from fossil fuel producers can be overcome. Attempts to undermine the work of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change must also be resisted. It provides the science on which the process depends. Increased accountability on climate finance is urgently needed too. Poor countries cannot be expected to put up with endless delays.

A small island community spent years preparing for the climate crisis. Now they have no water – and nowhere else to go




Visitors are few to the island of Ahus, a tiny atoll in the north of Papua New Guinea’s sprawling archipelago.
But Prof Josh Cinner and his team are well known. The ocean sustainability researchers have been visiting the island for a quarter of a century, their arrivals usually heralded with a modest ceremony, dancing and shared food and drink.

The last time they arrived – in October – it was “a ghost town”.
“The research team wondered if everyone was off-island,” Cinner, director of the University of Sydney’s Thriving Oceans Research Hub, tells the Guardian, “but then they would look in the houses and just see people lying on the ground of their huts, trying to conserve energy, trying to conserve water.

“School was cut to a half day … because it was too hot for the kids to be in school, and there’s been a massive reduction in fishing. Fishing is very physical, and people just don’t have enough water, they don’t have enough energy, and it’s just too hot to go fishing.”


PNG, and a huge swathe of south-east Asia, is in the grip of a brutal “supercharged” El Niño event, that has brought soaring temperatures, vanishingly little rain and widespread food and water shortages.
The drought has meant that on the neighbouring, larger island of Manus, there is little food on sale at the markets. But the fishers of Ahus have few fish to trade anyway.
The intensely interconnected economy which has sustained these islands for generations is breaking down.
“When it finally did rain, everyone was excited,” Cinner says. “But there’s all this smoke from the bushfires in Borneo, it’s just haze. So when the rain came, it was acid rain.”

“What could prepare you for this? Even the rain in a drought is toxic,” Cinner says. “What do you do? The wells are dry. They have to paddle across the channel to try to get water on the mainland [Manus Island], but they don’t have rights to the water there. And the creeks there are drying out.”

articles.jina_text:
The UN’s annual climate conference began in Turkey this week. Reporting from the event can be gruelling work – but it’s also crucial. 




They are counting on you not to read our coverage of the Cop31 climate talks. Fossil fuel companies, climate science deniers, petrostates, far right populists … They want you to think the negotiations are too intractable, the progress too halting, the issues too complex, too tortuous, too pointless, TL;DR.
But as the UN’s 31st annual climate conference got underway in Antalya, Turkey this week, our journalists have been going to great lengths to help you understand why the talks remain urgent, crucial and – hopefully – consequential. As well as helping you follow the agreements reached and progress made during the two week summit, they have also been highlighting what’s at stake.








What’s the point? Ten years after the Paris treaty, are climate talks getting anywhere?

Read more
Covering a Cop is gruelling work. The negotiations are by definition difficult: representatives from almost every country in the world attempt to thrash out consensus agreements and roadmaps for confronting humanity’s greatest threat. There are also practical hurdles, with 70,000 registered delegates at this year’s summit, packed venues and tangled schedules. On Tuesday morning, the Guardian’s live blog from the conference also chronicled the odyssey of our journalist Graham Readfearn as he struggled for three and a half hours just to get to the venue on one of the special Cop31 buses that got caught in the Antalya traffic.
Graham’s quest wasn’t a metaphor – it was just one of many practical challenges reporters face when covering a Cop (which stands for Conference of the Parties to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change). These challenges are that much harder for smaller media organisations from poorer nations that are particularly vulnerable to the impacts of the climate emergency.
I asked some of our journalists ​why it’s such an important conference to cover and the challenges they face reporting from it.


Ajit Niranjan 
European environment correspondent
“The hardest thing about covering Cop is satisfying the many different audiences who turn to our coverage during this chaotic fortnight. For the tens of thousands of people attending the summit, we offer a close-up view of the diplomatic spats (and rare breakthroughs) that have sweeping consequences for humanity and the other species with which we share this planet. And for the average Guardian reader, who cares about the climate but may not need the minutiae of UN diplomacy, we mix key takeaways from the negotiations with the most riveting, heartbreaking, terrifying and encouraging stories about the climate crisis. It’s a rare moment during the year when climate change is in the spotlight, and we want to serve as many readers as we can.”

The latest Met Office forecast suggests hill snow across North Wales, northern England and Scotland from Tuesday, along with plunging temperatures throughout the UK. 
As winter approaches, many households will be thinking about turning their heating up to keep the cold at bay.  
But as energy costs continue to put pressure on household budgets — with the typical household paying around £144 a month for gas and electricity — finding ways to stay warm without sending bills soaring is more important than ever. 

 

Thankfully however, there are a few simple things you can do before the cold snap hits to improve your heating efficiency without spending a penny. 

 
Reduce your boiler flow temperature  
This tiny tweak can save £100 a year if you have a combi boiler – and you won’t notice the difference. 
Your boiler comes with a default ‘flow temperature’, which controls how hot the water is when it leaves your boiler to heat your radiators. 
According to Zoe Morris, savings expert at VoucherCodes.co.uk, most boilers are set to run at 70°C to 80°C, but they actually work more efficiently (and cheaply) at a lower temperature. 
‘By reducing the flow temperature to around 60°C, your boiler doesn’t have to work as hard, which means it uses less gas and, therefore, costs less to run,’ she told Metro. 
Lowering this setting means your boiler runs in its most efficient mode – known as condensing mode – which can significantly cut energy use. 
If you’re not sure how to do it, check the Money Saving Boiler Challenge from innovation charity Nesta or search online for videos that show your particular brand of boiler. 
 
   
Just a tiny tweak can save more than you would think (Picture: Getty Images) 
Get your radiators ready 
Cleaning and bleeding your radiators will help them work more efficiently, meaning you won’t have to use as much energy to get your rooms warm. 
British Gas repair engineer Sunny Solanky explains that pockets of air can build up inside radiators, preventing them from heating your home evenly. 
‘If you notice the top of your radiators feel cooler than the bottom, switch the system off and let it cool,’ he says. 
You can then use a radiator key to carefully release the trapped air, allowing hot water to circulate properly again. 

 
It’s also worth looking at what’s surrounding your radiators, as furniture can prevent heat from circulating around the room. 
Sebrina McCullough, of the Money Wellness blog, recommends leaving a little breathing room between your radiators and any furniture. 
She told Metro: ‘You should leave around 6in to 12in between any furniture and radiators to ensure free movement of air and circulation of heat.’ 
Lower the radiator valves in less-used rooms 
If you have thermostatic radiator valves (TRVs) fitted to your radiators, adjusting them could save you up to £40 a year, according to Smart Energy GB. 
These valves allow you to control the temperature of individual rooms, meaning you don’t have to heat every corner

articles.raw_rss: Dozens of homes in the east London borough are at risk of flooding, a new report has found

articles.jina_text:
A council leader has told of his relief that he no longer resides on a council estate now deemed a major flood risk zone. 




Barking and Dagenham Labour council leader Dominic Twomey has said he is “glad” he no longer lives on the Rylands Estate in Oval Road North, where he called home for “many years”.








He added he “would never have imagined” it would be part of an area at risk of flooding.




Cllr Twomey said: “I’m glad I no longer live where I used to live.




“Some of the areas here – middle of the borough – are not at risk from the rivers.




“But that flooding because of other drainage issues is quite a worrying development, particularly with the changing weather that’s now coming forward, you can see that flooding through drainage issues more and more and more.”




The estate is one of four areas in Barking and Dagenham borough facing a “significant” flood risk, according to a new council flood strategy.




The flooding risk at Rylands Estate comes from water diverted by flood defences at the River Beam and Wantz Stream, according to a new draft flood risk management strategy.




The strategy says that “properties at risk lie mainly on Ballards Close, Ballards Road and the eastern end of School Road” while “several further properties on Oval Road North” are also at risk.


Oval Road North, Dagenham 
Google




It adds that 16 homes could be flooded in a one-in-30 year flooding event.




Homes are at less risk from flooding around Parsloes Park – 76 homes could be flooded in a one-in-75 year event.












Elsewhere in the borough, some 48 homes are at risk around Heathway Industrial Estate – mainly on Rainham Road North and Panyers Gardens – because they sit on the historic path of the Wantz Stream, which is now diverted underground in a culvert.




Westrow Drive is also at risk of flooding by water diverted by flood defences elsewhere, with 18 homes at risk. 








The draft strategy says surface water flowing towards the Mayes Brook is blocked by a flood defence, causing it to “pond in the residential area behind it”.




The draft flood risk management strategy proposes four projects to protect homes in those areas. These include building a flood bank in Old Dagenham Park to protect Rylands Estate, at a cost of around £212,337.

The council has applied for grant funding for a flood water storage scheme in Rainham Road North.

‘Risk multiplier’: super El Niño looms over Cop31 as climate pattern fuels global disasters


Strongest El Niño in centuries adds urgency to UN climate talks as vulnerable countries face ‘compounding’ crises




If the galloping pace of the climate crisis isn’t enough to spur countries to act at UN climate talks under way in Turkey, there is another major threat heightening its havoc: the strongest El Niño event in at least 1,000 years.
The “jaw-dropping” El Niño, a naturally recurring phenomenon where the eastern Pacific heats up every few years with temporary but global implications, has provided added urgency to wrangling at the Cop31 summit over climate funding for vulnerable countries that are having to scramble to respond.

Already, warping global weather patterns have fuelled huge wildfires and crop failures in Indonesia, coastal inundation in the US, severe drought in Sudan and severe flooding in countries including Ecuador and Somalia. “We are supercharging our weather and El Niño will be a risk multiplier,” said Celeste Saulo, secretary-general of the World Meteorological Organization.






El Niño will increase risk of death in childbirth for millions, say midwives

Read more
Drought has ravaged the Marshall Islands, a small Pacific atoll country which relies heavily on rainfall for its water. “It’s a compounding crisis, we are trying to prepare but the drought has already hit and it’s on top of having to deal with rising seas that threaten our homes and drinking water,” said Kathy Jetn̄il-Kijiner, climate envoy for the Marshall Islands, which has declared a state of emergency.
Last year, wealthy countries agreed to triple the amount of adaptation finance to poorer countries most vulnerable to floods heatwaves, wildfires and other damaging climate impacts. Yet just a fraction of the $305bn a year needed by 2035 is being delivered, with rich nations consistently lagging in providing climate finance.
This shortfall will be sharply felt in the coming year as El Niño takes its toll. “It’s so frustrating as countries that have done the least to cause climate change are being left with bills we can’t afford,” said Jetn̄il-Kijiner.

articles.title: Youth benefits system needs ‘fundamental reset’, Cabinet minister warns

articles.raw_content:
Pat McFadden, the Work and Pensions Secretary, has said “we have to reorientate the system” to help young people out of unemployment.



Ahead of the Milburn review set to be published this week, McFadden told Sky News there must be a “fundamental reset” to implement the report’s findings.



This includes cutting welfare benefits to redirect the funds towards supporting young pople into work or training.



“If you have extra costs because of a condition, there will also be an extra cost benefit, and people will get investment in support upfront, as well as the benefit figures,” McFadden said.



“You’ve also got to consider the long-term consequences of being on those benefits. One of the most remarkable statistics I’ve come across in the last year is that if a young person goes on to long-term sickness benefits at the age of 20, they’re more likely to celebrate their 30th birthday than to have had a steady job in between.”
